one_liner: PHP extension: lock-free shared-memory key/value cache for FPM workers on one host, replacing local Memcached/APCu without a network hop.
what_it_does: Yac is a C extension for PHP (PECL/PIE) that keeps a user-data cache in a shared-memory segment created at module startup and inherited by every forked PHP-FPM worker, so any worker on the machine can read what another wrote. Its API is a `Yac` class with memcached-like add/set/get/delete/has/flush plus info/dump, multi-key array forms, TTL in seconds and a per-instance key prefix. It is not the Memcached client API, so application code or a framework adapter has to call it. The benchmarked setup used the author's separate wp-yac-cache plugin, a WordPress object-cache.php drop-in that maps wp_cache_* onto Yac.
how_it_is_fast: It removes the network: a get() is a MurmurHash64A lookup into a fixed power-of-two slot table in already-mapped memory. It probes at most 4 slots (home slot plus an odd stride) and copies the value out, with no socket, loopback TCP round trip or protocol encoding. Concurrency is lock-free. Each slot has a seqlock-style version counter: readers snapshot it and retry, and writers claim it with a CAS, giving up after 30 spins. Values sit in ring segments handed out by a CAS bump pointer. On every read a full CRC-32C check (SSE4.2 or ARMv8 hardware, detected at runtime) turns recycled or torn blocks into misses instead of taking a lock. Small scalars and strings up to 7 bytes are embedded in the slot's pointer word, and values that fit beside the key in the 48-byte key area are stored inline, so neither needs a value block. Values over 4K are LZ4-compressed by default.
when_to_use: A single PHP-FPM host, or a few independent ones, where Memcached or Redis on localhost serves only as a same-machine cache: the WordPress object cache, config, routing tables, rendered fragments.
Requests that do dozens to hundreds of cache gets each, where localhost TCP round trips per get add up. This is the WordPress case: about 19% more RPS even though the ceiling is set by PHP and MySQL.
Read-heavy access (the project's own benchmark uses 100:1 read:write) with many small values. Ints, bools, null and strings of 7 bytes or less live in the slot and skip value allocation entirely.
You would rather not run, secure and monitor a cache daemon, and losing the cache on every php-fpm restart is acceptable.
PHP 7.0-8.5 on Linux x86-64/ARM64 or Windows (both covered by CI), in NTS or ZTS builds.
when_not_to_use: Several web nodes that must see each other's writes or invalidations. Each host's segment is private, so a delete or flush on one node never reaches the others.

Sharing between unrelated processes such as cron jobs, standalone CLI scripts or a second FPM master. Only the process that created the segment and its forked children can attach to it (issue #124), and CLI is disabled by default.

Write-heavy or hot-key write workloads. set() returns false when it loses the slot CAS race, and the README says to avoid several processes setting the same key at once. The WordPress drop-in's incr/decr is a non-atomic get-then-set, so counters lose updates under concurrency.

Keys over 48 bytes (PSR-16 requires 64, issue #83), values over 64 MB raw or 1 MB after compression, or incompressible values above the compression threshold, where set() fails if LZ4 would make them bigger.

Risk-averse production that needs a long-settled engine. The storage layer was largely rewritten in Aug-Sep 2026 (2.4.0-2.4.2): 2.4.2 fixed a get() crash under concurrency and a flush() race that could leave a slot permanently unusable. In 2021 (issue #122) the author said the older partial-CRC Yac 'has a certain probability of error'.

integration.form: shared lib (PHP extension yac.so/.dll, installed via PECL, PIE or phpize; the WordPress path adds the wp-yac-cache plugin, which deploys wp-content/object-cache.php)
integration.dependencies: none required (LZ4 is bundled, or a system LZ4 via --with-system-lz4); optional msgpack, igbinary or json serializers. The WordPress plugin needs PHP 7.2+ and WordPress 5.6+.
integration.min_toolchain: PHP 7.0+ (package.xml; CI builds 7.0 through 8.5). A C compiler with the GCC/Clang __atomic/__sync builtins, or MSVC; configure fails otherwise. Needs mmap(MAP_ANON) or SysV shm.
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and ARM64 (CI, including a 30-second 16-worker concurrency hammer on both), Windows x64 and x86 (named file mapping), macOS (the author's benchmark machine, not in CI). Hardware CRC-32C is used when SSE4.2 or ARMv8 CRC is detected at runtime, with a slicing-by-8 software fallback otherwise.
integration.thread_safety: Safe across processes and ZTS threads through lock-free per-slot version counters (seqlock-style) with CAS claims, a CAS bump allocator and CRC-32C validation on every read. Writes can fail under contention and return false, and the README advises retrying and avoiding concurrent writers on the same key.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is neither wire- nor API-compatible with Memcached, so code must call the Yac class, whose add/set/get/delete-with-TTL semantics resemble memcached's. For WordPress, the wp-yac-cache drop-in replaces the Memcached object-cache drop-in with no code changes. However, wp_cache_flush_group only clears the request-local copy, and wp_cache_flush wipes the whole host's Yac memory.

gotchas: Yac::flush() (and so wp_cache_flush()) invalidates the entire shared segment on the host, across every prefix and every app attached to the same PHP master. delete() only writes a tombstone, and memory comes back only when the value ring wraps around.

Without a default argument, get() returns false for both a miss and a stored false; pass a sentinel default (2.4.0+) to tell them apart. Since 2.4.0, multi-get omits missing keys instead of returning false placeholders, so code that reads $result[$key] directly can raise warnings. The WordPress drop-in writes a stored false as 0.

In the WordPress drop-in, keys over the 48-byte budget have their key part replaced by a 32-bit crc32b hash and are not re-checked on read. Two long keys in the same group can therefore collide and silently return each other's value. A birthday estimate (derived, not documented) is about a 1% chance with ~10K live long keys in one group. Do not set yac.serializer=json for WordPress either: objects come back as arrays and cause fatal errors.

Capacity is fixed at startup. keys_memory_size sets the slot count (8M is about 64K slots), and each key can only occupy its 4 probe slots, so live entries can be kicked long before the table fills. A value bigger than one 4M+ segment fails (the 'fails' counter goes up). Size both pools from info() hit, kick and recycle counters.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Yac when the application is PHP-FPM. It is the only catalogued Memcached-beater whose cache lives in memory shared across forked PHP workers; CacheLib (in-process C++) and python-diskcache (in-process Python) are the equivalents for other runtimes. Stay with a networked cache such as Memcached, Pogocache or Dragonfly when more than one host has to share entries or invalidations.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's WordPress site (laruence.com; an 8-core/31 GB server running PHP 8.1 FPM behind Nginx; CPU model and compiler flags not stated), swapping the Memcached object-cache drop-in (memcached on localhost:11211) for the Yac drop-in raised full-homepage throughput from about 118.5 to about 141.5 RPS (+18.6% to +20.1%). It also cut p50 latency by about 16-17% at 20, 50 and 100 concurrent ab clients, with both setups capped by PHP rendering and MySQL; a fixed 10,000-request run gave +17.6%. Yac's own microbenchmark (16 forked workers, 100:1 read:write, Apple M5 Pro, PHP 8.5) reports 170-727x more aggregate ops/s than per-worker TCP connections to a local memcached 1.6.45, which mostly measures the removed loopback round trip rather than cache mechanics.
